title: the Ninefold Court Rising Again
premise: Tamsin Villalobos has survived fifteen years in the city of Vell by selling harmless charms and never once letting her beast-speaker gift show—until a mute child arrives at her door speaking the Old Tongue, the language animals answered before kingdoms existed. The child is a fragment of King Aldric's stolen memory, smuggled out by rebels who believe the thing wearing his crown, an ancient parasite called the Ninefold Court, can be unbound if its anchor—the king's buried love for a woman Tamsin unknowingly resembles—is restored. As Tamsin teaches the child to speak again and falls into dangerous alliance with the rebel Wren, she must choose between exposing her gift (and dying as all magic-bearers do) or letting Vell's last true king be devoured. In the end, Tamsin gives the Court her own memories of love in exchange for Aldric's freedom, surviving hollowed but not empty, because the child—and Wren—refuse to let her forget who she was.
about_author: Cyrus Underhill is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing extinct languages before turning to fiction. They write fantasy about memory, obligation, and the small magics people hide to survive.

chapters.title: The Charm Seller's Door
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet her careful, gray life in occupied Vell: selling luck-knots, hiding her gift even from herself, trading small words with street cats when no one watches. A knock at night reveals a child, silent, eyes old beyond years, clutching a scrap of cloth embroidered with a sigil Tamsin hasn't seen since her mother died. Emotional beat: dread dressed as routine cracking open.

chapters.title: A Language Older Than Kingdoms
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The child speaks one word aloud—a word in the Old Tongue—and every animal within three streets goes still. Tamsin realizes the child isn't cursed but remembering: a splinter of King Aldric's mind, hidden from the Ninefold Court. She should turn them away; instead she feeds them. Emotional beat: terror and tenderness arriving together.

chapters.title: What the Rats Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, first use of her full gift in fifteen years. She questions the city's rats and gulls, learning the Court hunts anything that speaks the Old Tongue—and that soldiers have begun sweeping the lower quarters. The child, named Ember by Tamsin, begins recalling fragments: a woman's laugh, a garden, a crown that whispers. Emotional beat: the past becoming lethal.

chapters.title: The Rebel Called Wren
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A rebel courier tracks the memory-fragment to Tamsin's shop, intending retrieval—or destruction if it's compromised. Instead she finds Tamsin defending Ember with a lie so smooth it frightens them both. Wren reveals the truth: the king lives, enthralled, and the fragment is his anchor to freedom. Emotional beat: wary alliance forged over shared risk.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, flashback-woven. We learn how her mother was burned for beast-speaking and how Tamsin swore invisibility, burying her gift like a body. Now teaching Ember words feels like exhuming it. Wren presses her to come to the rebels' crypt-hideout; Tamsin refuses—until soldiers burn the shop next door. Emotional beat: grief refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Crypt Beneath the Belltower
chapters.summary: Alternating Tamsin/Wren POV. In the rebels' hideout, Ember's memories sharpen: the Court entered the king through a vow he made at his coronation, and only someone the king loved can speak him free. The rebels look at Tamsin—at her face, so like the dead queen's—and understand why the fragment came to her door. Emotional beat: destiny felt as accusation.

chapters.title: The Court Wears Many Faces
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A traitor in the rebellion sells their location; the Court's enforcers, wearing the faces of trusted friends, breach the crypt. Ember is taken. Wren escapes with Tamsin, badly wounded, and confesses she was the one who sent the fragment to Tamsin—not fate, but a calculated gamble she now regrets. Emotional beat: betrayal inside devotion.

chapters.title: Into the Whispering Crown
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin walks willingly into the palace, posing as a charm-seller summoned to court, her beasts mapping every corridor. She reaches the throne room and meets King Aldric—hollow-eyed, nine voices layered under his own. The Court offers her a bargain: her silence forever, in exchange for walking away. Emotional beat: temptation of safe cowardice.

chapters.title: The Unbinding
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. Using the Old Tongue through Ember's rescued voice, Tamsin begins the unbinding—but the Court demands a memory-anchor of equal weight. She offers her own memories of love: her mother's songs, her growing bond with Wren and Ember. The Court, greedy, takes them all—and in taking them, loosens its grip on Aldric, who breaks free and shatters it. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the price of survival, paid in full.

chapters.title: What Remains When Memory Burns
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, resolution. The king lives, magic is still outlawed but no longer hunted to ash, and Tamsin remembers nothing of why she weeps at certain songs. Ember refuses to let her stay hollow, retelling her own story back to her day by day; Wren stays too, patient. The final scene: a cat speaks to Tamsin, and though she doesn't know the word for what she feels, she answers. Emotional beat: love rebuilding what sacrifice consumed.
